Conformity and Its Impact on Purchasing Decisions on Social Media
Andre Weiss, Anastasia Belyakov, Yashika S. Chari, Anna L. Mathew, Tyler M. Pauly, Marcela Perches, Diane Mello-Goldner, Ph.D.
Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Boston University
Abstract
This study explores how peer opinions on social media influence consumer behavior. One hundred and 
thirteen participants watched influencer-style videos expressing either positive, neutral, or negative opinions 
about a fictional water bottle, coined by researchers “AquaArmor,” followed by questions about purchasing 
intentions. Results showed no correlation between peer opinions and purchasing behavior. However, 
positive stimuli notably increased purchasing intentions, including a willingness to pay higher prices, 
compared to neutral or negative stimuli. Gender differences were observed, with males showing higher 
purchasing intent, particularly after exposure to positive videos. Owing to the limitation of the study as 
discussed further research is needed to understand the mechanisms behind consumer conformity.
Introduction
This study expands on previous research to examine how conformity to peer opinions and trends on social 
media affects purchasing behaviors and brand perceptions. We aimed to answer the question: "How does 
conformity to peer opinions and trends on social media influence purchasing behaviors and brand 
perceptions?" We hypothesized that greater conformity scores will have a positive impact, based on social 
influence patterns (Wang et al., 2021) and the role of social validation in consumer decisions (Mallinson and 
Hatemi, 2018). 
Method
Participants
One-hundred and thirteen participants (80 females, 30 males, mean age = 22, SD = 1.99) completed the 
survey after watching a promotional video. 
Materials
Participants completed a Qualtrics survey comprising pretest and post-test sections, along with a 30 to 45-
second TikTok-style promotion of an unnamed water bottle, randomly assigned as positive, negative, or 
neutral. The advertisement was experimentally designed and followed a typical user-generated format. 
Participants also completed additional questions, including an adapted peer pressure inventory scale 
(Cronbach’s α = 0.77).
Procedure
Participants provided consent and answered demographic and water bottle purchasing questions. They 
viewed the promotional video and then completed a post-test survey assessing their perception of the bottle. 
Participants were randomly assigned to experimental groups via Qualtrics. Following the video, they were 
asked about purchasing intent based on pseudo-statistics matching the video's opinion. Participants also 
completed an adapted peer pressure inventory scale. After completion, participants were thanked and 
debriefed.
Figure 1
Video Actress with “AquaArmor” Water Bottle
Results
Our study explored the relationship between peer opinions, social media trends, and consumer behaviors. 
Although correlation analyses did not find a direct link between conformity to peer opinions on social media 
and purchasing behaviors, the absence of correlation might indicate the presence of other factors.
Positive valence videos notably increased purchase intentions, confirmed through consistent participant 
responses with a high Cronbach’s α value. The shift in intentions from pre- to post-video viewing highlighted 
the impact of exposure to positive feedback videos, emphasizing the role of emotional context in persuasion, 
supported by the substantial effect size indicated by Cramer's V . Moreover, our study emphasized the 
influence of positive valenced videos on purchasing attitudes, affirming that products associated with positive 
opinions are more likely to attract consumer interest and command higher prices. These findings underscore 
the importance of positive sentiment in shaping consumer behaviors and suggest the potential effectiveness of 
leveraging positivity in promotional campaigns.The predominantly female sample may have skewed 
observed gender differences in purchasing intentions, highlighting the need for balanced samples in future 
research. Additionally, the inclusion of a fictitious statistic alongside the advertisement could have influenced 
participant attitudes. Moreover, using a preexisting product might have introduced biases in participants' 
purchasing decisions.
Despite these limitations, our findings have significant implications for marketing strategies. Understanding 
the role of positive emotions in consumer behaviors informs effective communication strategies and 
facilitates constructive interactions. Our study also sheds light on mechanisms behind conformity in 
consumerism, paving the way for further exploration of purchase intentions in the digital age.
A two-way factorial ANOV A was employed to explore potential gender differences and the influence of 
video valences on purchase intentions. A main effect of gender was observed, F(1,105)= 7.94, p = 0.006, η2 = 
.07, indicating males exhibited higher purchase intentions than females. Moreover, a main effect of video 
valences was evident, F(1, 105) = 13.66, p < 0.001, η2 = .21, signifying that positive video stimuli elicited 
the greatest increase in purchase intention. However, no significant interaction effect was detected 
between gender and video valances (refer to Table 4).
Table 4
Means and Standard Deviations for Purchase Intention based on Gender Differences and Stimuli
Note. Marginal means are provided for average purchase intentions across gender. 
Willingness to Pay
Furthermore, a chi-square test of independence was conducted to explore the association between video 
valences and participants willingness to pay. Notably, a significant relationship emerged, χ2(6) = 23.47, p < 
.001, Cramer’s V = .32, indicating that participants exposed to positive video stimuli demonstrated a 
higher willingness to pay compared to those exposed to neutral or negative videos (refer to Table 5).
Table 5
Percentages of Participants’ Perception of Price Based on Video Valence
Note. Relevant water bottle examples were used for price comparisons.
Impressions of Water Bottle
Upon viewing the video valances, participants were asked about their impressions of the water bottle. Table 
1 shows the distribution of participant impressions across different video conditions. Largely, participants 
exposed to positive videos reported positive impressions, mirroring similar trends in the neutral and negative 
conditions, χ2(4) = 45.78, p < .001, Cramer’s V = .45. Particularly, the negative condition elicited primarily 
negative perceptions.
Purchase Intention
Differences in pre- and post-test purchase intentions following exposure to the video valences were 
examined to explore any association with peer pressure scale scores. No significant correlation was 
discerned between these variables, r(108) = -.01, p = .95.
An ANOV A was performed to investigate the influence of different video valences on participant’s attitudes 
toward purchasing the water bottle. The analysis unveiled significant disparities in purchasing attitudes 
among participants exposed to positive, negative, and neutral videos, F(2, 110) = 18.18, p < .001, η2 = .25. 
Subsequent post-hoc tests revealed that participants exposed to positive videos exhibited higher 
purchasing intentions compared to those exposed to neutral or negative videos (refer to Table 2).
Another ANOV A was conducted to assess whether the video conditions impacted changes in purchase 
intentions from pre- to post-testing. Results indicated a notable effect of the videos on purchase intentions, 
F(2, 110) = 16.76, p < .001, Î·2 = .23. Post-hoc analyses further revealed that participants exposed to 
positive videos displayed elevated purchasing intentions relative to those exposed to neutral or 
negative videos (refer to Table 3).

Large Language Models for Zero-Shot Procedure Extraction in Orthopedic
Surgery: A Comparative Evaluation
Ashton Williamson, M.S. 1, Nazgol Tavabi, Ph.D.1, Nishita Kalepalli, M.S. 1, Ophelie Lavoie-Gagne, M.D. 1, Andre
Weiss, B.S.1, Benjamin Owens, M.S. 2, Andrew Sibley, B.S. 2, Rafael A. Garc ´ ıa And´ ujar, B.S.1, Alexandra Santos,
B.S.1, Alex Kim, B.S. 1, Mahad M Hassan, M.D. 1,2,3, and Ata M. Kiapour, Ph.D., M.M.Sc. 1,4,*
1Department of Orthopedics and Sports Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston,
MA 02115, United States
2Department of Orthopedic Surgery, University of Minnesota, Minneapolis, MN 55454, United States
3Department of Orthopedic Surgery, TRIA Orthopaedic Center, Bloomington, MN 55122, United States
4Harvard Data Science Initiative, Harvard University, Allston, MA 02134, United States
*Corresponding Author: Ata M. Kiapour (ata.kiapour@childrens.harvard.edu)
Abstract
Operative notes in electronic health records contain critical information for understanding surgical
care, yet manual coding is time-consuming, costly, and inconsistent. Large language models (LLMs)
promise to transform this process by automatically extracting detailed procedure information —a capa-
bility with significant implications for scaling clinical registries and advancing surgical research. Here,
we conducted a large-scale evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs for zero-shot structured information ex-
traction from orthopedic clinical notes. Fourteen open-source and proprietary models were tested on
800 real operative notes, annotated by both an orthopedic surgeon and an administrator using a curated
list of 74 procedure classes. We compared model outputs to human annotations, assessing accuracy
and exploring the effects of model scale, reasoning capabilities, and prompt design. We find that across
models, LLMs consistently outperform administrator-assigned labels, achieving macro-F1 scores above
0.6 and improving over administrative coding by up to 10 points. Larger models and reasoning capabil-
ities further boosted performance, though gains plateaued beyond 30 billion parameters. Performance
varied by procedure frequency, revealing clear strengths and persistent challenges for rare or complex
cases. Modern LLMs can already outperform routine administrative coding in extracting detailed surgical
procedure data, pointing to a future where registry curation could be faster, cheaper, and more consis-
tent. Yet, full alignment with surgical experts remains an open challenge—especially for rare procedures
—emphasizing the need for domain adaptation and thoughtful deployment. Our findings illustrate how
general-purpose LLMs can advance automated clinical data curation and inform the next generation of
surgical informatics.
Introduction
Clinical registries, also referred to as patient or disease registries, are organized repositories of patient data
that are collected through observational means for an express purpose.1 The construction of clinical registries
has emerged as a critical task in healthcare with the potential to enhance clinical research, improve patient
quality of care and treatment outcomes, and reduce the cost burden of healthcare. 2–5 Despite these benefits,
the deployment of clinical registries is often hindered by the high costs associated with implementation and
maintenance. In a recent survey of organizations operating clinical registries, 64% listed cost as a barrier
to sustainability while another survey of high-risk device registries found that only half of respondents
received sustainable registry funding.6,7 One potential avenue for mitigating the high financial cost of registry
construction is the use of secondary data sources, particularly data captured within the electronic health
record (EHR) system. While the process of transforming EHR data to fit a registry schema is straightforward
for structured data, it is significantly more challenging for unstructured data, like clinical notes. Transforming
unstructured clinical notes into variables of interest in the registry is a task that has traditionally necessitated
skilled human abstractors, in a process commonly referred to as chart review. Machine-learning-based natural
language processing (NLP) algorithms have provided a promising alternative to this paradigm by improving
ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
ARTICLE IN PRESSARTICLE IN PRESS

the cost burden, turnaround time, and overall accuracy but are often limited in practice by the need for
annotated, in-domain training data.8–11. Recent work has highlighted the potential of large language models
(LLMs) to further expedite the registry creation process by circumventing the need for tailored training
data.12–15 Questions remain, however, as to the robustness of these approaches to task complexity, label
space dimensionality, variations in medical subdomains and other implementation challenges.
In this work we investigate the extent to which LLMs can assist in the creation and curation of clini-
cal registries by evaluating their ability to extract clinically significant variables from unstructured medical
notes in a zero-shot setting. We construct a dataset consisting of operative notes drawn from a high-volume
hip-preservation clinic that treats children and young adults, a setting that introduces additional hetero-
geneity in diagnoses, operative techniques, and documentation styles. We select this domain deliberately
because hip surgeries are both common and clinically complex, often involving several different simultaneous
procedures. While recent studies have applied large language models to either procedural coding or free-text
information extraction (for example, named-entity recognition), these approaches often fall short for large-
scale clinical analysis because raw extracted spans can be inconsistent, ambiguous, or difficult to aggregate.
In practice, downstream applications such as registries require consistent, standardized representations of
complex procedures. This need is especially acute in domains like orthopedic hip surgery, where common
CPT codes may group together distinct operations —such as open femoral head/neck osteochondroplasty,
open labral repair, periacetabular osteotomy, and triple innominate osteotomy —under the same code, ob-
scuring important procedural differences.16 To address this, we framed the task not as open-ended extraction,
but as multi-label classification into a carefully defined set of orthopedic procedure classes. This approach
bridges the gap between LLMs’ ability to parse rich procedural detail and the practical requirement for
structured, analyzable data. This presents a departure from previous work in LLM-based procedure clas-
sification from orthopedic operative notes, which focused solely on CPT-code classification for a set spinal
surgery related CPT codes. 17 Our contributions include the following:
1. We perform a large-scale evaluation of state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs) for zero-shot
multi-label classification of orthopedic operative notes to support clinical registry construction.
2. We develop and utilize an expert-annotated dataset covering 74 procedure classes across 800 real-world
operative notes.
3. We demonstrate that modern LLMs consistently outperform administrator-assigned procedure labels,
with the best model improving macro-F1 by 0.10.
4. We analyze the effect of model scaling on performance and efficiency and show diminishing returns be-
yond 30 billion parameters, while highlighting the benefit of reasoning capabilities (“thinking tokens”)
and the impact of different prompting strategies.
5. We leverage our pipeline to construct a comprehensive, 20-year registry of over 80,000 hip procedures
across thousands of pediatric patients, which is currently supporting multiple ongoing clinical research
efforts.
Results
Dataset
The test set consisted of 800 operative notes, each from a distinct patient and hospital encounter, from 2000
to 2023. Average note length was approximately 1057 tokens (using the GPT-4o tokenizer) with a standard
deviation of 913 tokens. In the expert-annotated evaluation set, 90% of the procedure classes (66/74) occur
at least once, with an average of 2.64 procedure classes per operative note ( ±2.15) and a maximum of 13
procedure classes assigned to a single note. We calculate Krippendorf’s Alpha for the expert-annotated and
administrator-annotated evaluation sets, which we find to be α = 0.714.
Zero Shot Multilabel Procedure Classification
Multilabel classification on the expert annotated set was run across all the models in Table 2. In order
to compare the performance across different models we ranked them in terms of F1-score using a Critical

rank test with Holm’s Correction. Full results of all models across all metrics can be found in Supplementary

Discussion
The extraction of structured data elements from unstructured text within the Electronic Health Record
System is a critical task with the potential to enhance the precision of clinical decision-making by enabling
large-scale analyses of patient data. While large language models have gained popularity on the task of struc-
tured data retrieval in the medical domain, 19–21 the extent to which models can replace expert annotation
remains unclear, particularly in specialized sub-domains for which benchmark data is scarce. In this study
we investigated the alignment of large language models with human annotators of varying levels of expertise
on the task of classifying hip procedures performed in orthopedic hip operations using associated operative
notes. Our approach was later used to build a registry of over 20 years of data, capturing 86,555 distinct hip
procedures across more than 12,000 patients, with an average age of 14 (See Appendix L in Supplementary
Materials for more details). This process completed in under just two hours using GPT-OSS-120B, compared
to our human annotators for which the same task took weeks for a dataset of less than 3% of the size.
Our annotation strategy used two complementary annotator roles: an administrator annotator and a
pediatric orthopedic hip preservation expert. This design reflects a clinically realistic abstraction workflow,
in which administrative personnel may perform initial data extraction while domain experts provide reference
interpretation for specialized clinical classification tasks. However, each annotator role was represented by
a single annotator. As a result, although we can compare administrator and expert labels, we cannot fully
characterize within-role variability or estimate how labels might vary across multiple independent experts.
This limitation is relevant for operative-note classification, where ambiguous procedure descriptions may
support more than one plausible label. Given the specialized expertise required and the time-intensive
nature of annotation, additional independent expert annotation was not feasible in this study. Future
work with multiple expert annotators across institutions would further evaluate annotation variability and
generalizability.
While GPT-o4-mini demonstrates the best performance on the expert annotated set, the difference be-
tween the top-performing models across all procedure classes is not statistically significant and a number of
smaller, open-source models perform comparably. Among these models, we note three factors that generally
lead to enhanced performance: model size as measured by total parameters, test-time compute scaling with
thinking tokens, and training data tailored to the medical domain. While the positive association between
F1 performance and total parameters is not unexpected, it is worth noting the diminishing returns in model
size. Similarly, models that utilize reasoning capabilities or are trained primarily on medical data tend to
demonstrate better performance on the evaluation set. This comes at the cost of additional output tokens
(reasoning tokens) resulting in decreased overall throughput and increased financial cost if using the model
through a paid API with a token-based pricing model. Improving performance through opting for reasoning
models or increasing the reasoning token budget thus becomes an obvious choice in deployment environ-
ments where registry data is processed in an offline setting—in which inference is batched and latency is
not a concern—and where the LLM is self-hosted, in order to mitigate the financial penalty incurred by the
longer responses.
All approaches demonstrate a high level of per-procedure performance variability, excelling at identifying
some procedures while consistently struggling on others. While some of this inter-class performance disparity
is model dependent, we find some procedures to be consistently challenging for all LLMs. One example is the
set of open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) procedures, for which the mean macro-F1 across models
was less than 0.25. We find that this is most often due to ambiguous references to femoral fracture locations
in the notes (which are necessary for classification of 4 out of 7 of these procedures) as well as inconsistent
documentation of ORIF procedures by surgeons. We also note the challenge of distinguishing between similar
class names for different procedures—for example, periacetabular osteotomy and acetabular osteoplasty. We
find that providing the entire list of classes is necessary to allow the LLM to discriminate between multiple
similar classes, as evidenced by the decrease in precision resulting from providing individual classes for
classification in isolation. Despite the zero-shot nature of the prompting strategy, all models exhibit at least
a slight positive correlation between F1-score and procedure frequency in the expert-annotated test set (see
Appendix G for a plot of Matthew’s Correlation Coefficient vs Label Frequency). Although we suspect that
this discrepancy can be contributed to either shortcomings of the label taxonomy or annotation bias, we do
not discard the possibility that the LLMs may have had more exposure to the more common procedures in
their training corpus, leading to an increased familiarity with these classes.
While even state-of-the-art models failed to achieve high alignment with our expert annotator on the

evaluation set, we emphasize the importance of evaluating against annotators with less expertise, given the
practical realities of chart review implementation. To this end, we find that state-of-the-art, proprietary
LLMs outperform the administrative annotator when evaluating against an expert annotator on the task of
orthopedic hip procedure classification. Perhaps more surprising, however, is that all but two out of thirteen
models outperformed the administrative annotator on the expert set. This includes models with just 27
billion parameters, or approximately 4% of the size of the largest open-source LLM tested.
These findings support the potential utility of LLMs in clinical information extraction and, ultimately,
in creating and maintaining clinical registries. The minor relative difference in metric performance between
the top open weight models and state of the art proprietary models further suggests the viability of efficient,
on-premises deployment alternatives for clinical information extraction. Nonetheless, challenges remain in
incorporating these systems into real-world clinical workflows. For one, it can be challenging to quantify
uncertainty in model predictions, making it difficult to identify samples or individual predictions in need
of further manual review. While this may hinder integration into human-in-the-loop systems, it does not
entirely preclude it. As human-assistance tools in the clinical information extraction process, LLMs enable
systems for online annotation suggestions was well as retroactive error identification—both essential methods
for streamlining registry curation. Likewise, ethical concerns in unsupervised LLM deployment remain a
principal dilemma. Given the lack of explainability of these systems, comprehensive evaluation and continued
oversight are paramount to ensure equitable operation.
There are a few key limitations to this study. We first note the relatively small size of the dataset and the
lack of multi-institutional data, which both serve to limit the generalizability of our results. Additionally,
we emphasize that both our expert-annotated set and our administrator-annotated set are annotated by
individual annotators as opposed to multiple annotators, which we highlight as a fundamental limitation
of this study. Finally, we note the inherent limitations of assigning a discrete taxonomy to complex and
varied medical procedures. We conjecture that more well-defined rules for procedure assignment and more
transparent class definitions would lead to better replicability in the annotation process.
Methods
Dataset
The present study was reviewed by the Boston Children’s Hospital Institutional Review Board, who de-
termined that it met the criteria for exemption and waived the requirement of obtaining informed consent
(IRB-P00046914). All methods were conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines and regulations. Fol-
lowing approval, we obtained notes from all Boston Children’s Hospital clinics spanning 2000–2023. Using
a supervised machine learning pipeline developed in-house, 8 we filter out operative notes to include only
hip-related operations. This process yielded 30,192 operative notes for 12,203 unique patients across 22,415
encounters. In parallel, with input from a team of orthopedic surgeons, we manually curated a detailed set
of common hip procedures with focus on ensuring uniqueness, relevance, and comprehensive coverage. We
first constructed a candidate set of procedures using procedure data from internally-maintained surgical reg-
istries. This set was reviewed independently by a team of hip surgeons, who proposed additional procedure
classes as well as omissions of obsolete procedures and consolidations of functionally identical procedures.
The resulting set was edited to maintain consistent naming conventions. The final set comprised 74 distinct
surgical procedures (the full list of procedures is provided in Appendix A of Supplementary Materials).
Due to the expected long-tail distribution of our labels and the strong effect of sampling on evaluation
outcomes,22–24 we developed a targeted approach to increase representation of less common classes in the
evaluation set. We first embed all documents using doc2vec, 25 then cluster using k-means (with k equal
to the number of desired samples), and, finally, sample a single document from within each cluster with
probability proportional to their distance from the centroid (for more information on the sampling method,
see Supplementary Materials Appendix B). Using this method, we selected 800 operative notes for manual
annotation (dataset and sampled-set information, including counts, patient demographics, and note charac-
teristics, are provided in Table 3 of Appendix C in the Supplementary Materials). To assess model alignment
with domain experts of varying experience, the sampled notes were annotated once by an orthopedic surgeon
and once by an orthopedic administrator with over 10 years of experience, including in conducting chart
review. Annotators were each tasked with assigning binary procedure labels to each of the operative notes in
the dataset, corresponding to whether the procedure class was conducted as a procedure in the described op-

Given an operative note, the goal is to classify the procedures in the operative note into any of the
procedure classes without access to external knowledge sources or reference examples. Models are provided
with a description of the task along with a list of the procedure classes and prompted to return a JSON
object containing a key for each of the procedures and a binary value corresponding to whether a procedure
belonging to the class occurred in the operation. Model output is parsed to generate a label vector, where each
element corresponds to the presence of a particular procedure from the ordered list of candidate procedures.
We experiment with several different open-source LLMs as well as two closed-source, proprietary LLMs
(see Table 2). All open-source LLMs are run using the VLLM library on eight NVIDIA H200 GPUs using
default sampling parameters suggested by the respective model authors. Proprietary OpenAI models are
accessed through a HIPAA-secure institutional API. Models are evaluated against the annotated evaluation
set using macro- and micro-averaged Matthew’s Correlation Coefficient, F1, and accuracy. Given the long-
tail distribution of procedures in our evaluation dataset, we additionally provide an analysis of per-class
performance.
Model Comparison and Performance Analysis
The proliferation of both open-source and proprietary LLMs and the saturation of many common benchmarks
has come to complicate the process of choosing an LLM, particularly in lower-resource settings. To assess
the extent to which model architecture and design choices affect performance on our dataset, we evaluate
the impact of model size (measured in total model parameters), use of reasoning tokens, and differences
in computation time across models. Additionally, given the recent success of reasoning models, a term
which we use to refer to models that leverage thinking tokens in their responses, 33 we evaluate the extent
to which reasoning ability improves performance on our expert-annotated test set. We evaluate both the

stopping. Finally, we evaluate the effect of increased exposure to medical data during model training by
comparing the performance of two models of identical architecture trained on general domain (Gemma) and
biomedical datasets (MedGemma).
Prompting Strategies
Figure 5: A comparison of system prompts used for multi-label (our default task prompt, left) and single-
label (right) classification experiments. The procedure(s) variable is inserted dynamically at runtime.
Given the potentially long operative notes and the large number of procedure labels ( > 70), both the
input and expected output for the LLMs can be extensive. Since LLMs have been shown to be susceptible to
perturbations in prompt setup,34 we tested different prompting strategies and measured their impact on task
performance. The first of these was single-label classification, in which the LLM is provided a full operative
note and a single procedure to classify, instead of the full list of procedures (for a comparison of the prompts,
see Figure 5). While multilabel classification is a more intuitive approach to the task, it is possible that
the complexity introduced by the multilabel prompting setup could adversely affect performance. Providing
individual classes, in comparison, may be a more manageable task for an LLM.
The second approach was procedure span classification, in which the structured procedures performed
field is used in place of the entire document. In the US, operative notes tend to adhere to a template with
predefined fields for procedural details that are required for billing and reporting. This includes, at minimum,
patient information, surgery date and time, names of surgical staff, pre- and post-op diagnoses, procedure(s)
performed, anesthesia type, complications, implants, and procedural details. [35] For the task of procedure
classification, two of these sections appear to be the most relevant: procedures performed and procedural
details. The former of these is a more structured field containing a free-text list of procedures performed
(e.g. ”1. Removal of hardware, left hip 2. Wound irrigation”) while the latter contains a detailed, long-form
description of the specifics of the operation (an example de-identified operative note is provided in Figure 2
of Appendix C in the Supplementary Materials). For all other experiments, the full content of the operative
note is provided to the LLM as context. To text the extent to which the procedures performed section could
act as a stand in for the full text, we extracted the procedures performed field from the operative note and
provided it to the LLM in place of the full text. In effect, this approach both reduces overall input length
and reduces the noise introduced by the full body of the operative note, providing a brief clear summary of
the operation performed, at the expense of comprehensiveness. Full details of these approaches are provided
in the Supplementary Materials Appendices I and J.
